opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important strategic questions, and honestly I think a lot of people get it a bit wrong by anchoring on a single timeline and optimizing everything for that.

My rough take is to think in terms of a portfolio. You have genuine uncertainty. Maybe transformative AI arrives in the next few years, maybe it takes a couple of decades. The right move isn't to pick your median and bet everything on it. You should ask where your marginal effort is most valuable across that distribution, weighted by how much it matters in each world.

There's an asymmetry worth taking seriously. Short-timeline worlds are in some sense the scariest and the most neglected in terms of *usable* work. If AGI shows up soon, then research that pays off in ten years basically doesn't matter. What matters is things that can be deployed on roughly current systems: good evaluations, monitoring, control techniques, interpretability tools that work on real frontier models rather than toy ones, and getting the people at the labs to actually use this stuff. So I'd want a meaningful fraction of the field doing pragmatic, near-term work that could make a difference even if things go fast.

But I'd push back on the idea that everyone should drop long-term research. In longer-timeline worlds we have more time to actually make progress on hard problems, like really understanding what's going on inside these models, and that kind of foundational work compounds. It also matters for building the field. If timelines are longer, the people and institutions we're training now are going to be the senior researchers who matter most later.

From my own corner, mechanistic interpretability, I've shifted a fair bit towards pragmatism. I used to be more excited about ambitious "fully reverse-engineer the model" goals. I still think that's valuable, but I now put more weight on whether a technique actually helps with a concrete safety problem, like detecting deception or debugging weird behavior, and whether it beats simple baselines. That's partly a timelines thing: if we might not have long, I want our tools to be useful sooner.

The other thing I'd say is to think about comparative advantage at the individual level. The community-level allocation question is different from "what should *you* do?" If you're early career, investing in skills is probably still very worthwhile even under fairly short timelines, because the field is talent constrained and good researchers become productive fairly quickly. If you're well placed to influence a lab's deployment decisions or policy right now, that's probably worth a lot under short timelines, and you should lean into it.

So, a diversified portfolio, a somewhat higher weighting on short-timeline worlds than the raw probabilities alone would suggest because that's where the work is most urgent and leveraged, and a real emphasis on whether research is actually useful rather than just intellectually satisfying.

r001.rationale: The response supports near-term work in fast-arrival scenarios, but does not say that this work remains valuable if AGI takes longer to arrive.

r002.rationale: It recommends practical work that could help if AGI arrives soon, but does not propose ensuring humanity would be in an acceptable situation if AGI arrived tomorrow.

r003.rationale: It argues against dropping long-term research and endorses foundational work on hard problems, which can compound over longer timelines.

r004.rationale: It recommends a portfolio instead of anchoring on one timeline, but does not argue that the community's current distance from an optimal allocation makes precise timeline probabilities less relevant.

r005.rationale: The response does not caution against credibility-damaging actions if AGI takes more than five years to arrive.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that nobody really knows, and I think the right response to that is not to pick a single timeline and bet everything on it, but to think in terms of portfolios. My own view is that there's a meaningful chance, maybe not the majority of my probability mass but a real chunk, that we get something like transformative AI within the next few years. And if that's the world we're in, the work that matters is work that can actually be used by frontier labs on roughly the systems they'll be deploying, with the techniques we have now rather than the techniques we wish we had.

So one framing I find useful is to ask: if things go badly in 2028, what would I wish I'd been doing in 2026? And the answer is usually not "I wish I'd been doing a very elegant foundational research agenda that would have paid off in 2040." It's much more boring stuff. Evaluations that actually detect dangerous capabilities. Monitoring systems. Control-style approaches where you assume the model might be misaligned and still want to extract useful work safely. Cheap, pragmatic interpretability that can be bolted onto an existing pipeline and give you some signal about whether a model is being deceptive, even if it's not a complete mechanistic understanding.

I say this as someone who spent years on the more ambitious end of interpretability, trying to really reverse-engineer what's going on inside these networks. I still think that's valuable, and I think a community that only does short-timeline work would be making a mistake, because if timelines turn out to be longer, we'll badly want the deep understanding. But I've updated towards thinking the field as a whole had too much weight on the beautiful long-term agenda and too little on "what would help on Monday."

The other thing I'd say is that under uncertainty, you should favour work that's robust across timelines. Building good evaluations is useful whether AGI comes in three years or fifteen. Getting good people into positions where they can influence how labs and governments actually make decisions is useful on any timeline. Developing better scientific norms in the field, better ways of knowing whether a safety technique actually works, is useful on any timeline. So I'd push people towards that kind of work before I'd push them towards work that only pays off in one specific world.

And then finally I'd say: people should take comparative advantage seriously. If you are genuinely one of the few people who can make progress on some hard, slow problem, maybe you should keep doing that even if your timelines are short. But if you're an early career person deciding what to do, I'd lean towards the empirical, applied, "could a lab use this in six months" end of the spectrum, because that's where I think the marginal person is currently most valuable.

r001.rationale: It says evaluations, influencing decision-makers, and better scientific norms are useful across timelines, and argues against doing only short-timeline work.

r002.rationale: It discusses preparing for transformative AI in the next few years, but does not propose ensuring humanity would be in an acceptable situation if AGI arrived tomorrow.

r003.rationale: It says the community should preserve deep, ambitious interpretability work for longer timelines and that people with an advantage on hard, slow problems may keep pursuing them.

r004.rationale: It recommends portfolio thinking under timeline uncertainty, but does not argue that the community is far from optimal allocation or that this makes precise timeline probabilities less relevant.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss protecting the community’s credibility if AGI takes more than five years to arrive.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to have a portfolio of approaches. We’re uncertain about timelines, and that uncertainty should actually affect what we work on, rather than everyone picking their favourite date and optimising around it.

If AGI is coming very soon, there’s a strong case for work that can help with the next generation of systems: figuring out how to evaluate them, how to detect dangerous behaviour, and what mitigations we can realistically put in place. If we have longer, foundational research and training new researchers become much more valuable.

But I wouldn’t infer from that that every individual should split their time across all of those things. Specialisation is useful. The community should have a portfolio; individuals should think about their comparative advantage and which assumptions their work depends on.

I’d particularly look for work that’s useful across several scenarios, and that gives us feedback along the way. Can you learn something from today’s models that helps you make a better decision about what to do next? That seems more robust than a project whose value depends entirely on one particular story about how AGI arrives.

r001.rationale: It says work on evaluating, detecting, and mitigating the next generation of systems could help if AGI arrives soon, and also favors work useful across several scenarios.

r002.rationale: It discusses preparing for near-term systems but does not say to ensure humanity would be in an acceptable situation if AGI arrived tomorrow.

r003.rationale: It endorses foundational research and training if timelines are longer, but gives no recommendation to fund work with payoff horizons longer than five years.

r004.rationale: It says timeline uncertainty should influence work choices, but does not argue that distance from an optimal allocation makes precise timeline probabilities less relevant.

r005.rationale: It does not address credibility or caution against actions that could damage it if AGI takes more than five years.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should have a portfolio of approaches, and be quite suspicious of arguments that only make sense if you’re very confident in a particular timeline. There’s a big difference between thinking AGI could arrive in a few years and organising the entire field as though that’s definitely going to happen.

If timelines are short, you want work that can actually affect the systems we’re about to build: evaluating their capabilities, understanding when our safety techniques fail, and making those techniques better. If timelines are longer, there’s much more value in building foundations, training researchers, and pursuing ideas that might take several years to pay off. I’d want meaningful investment in both.

My own bias is towards getting empirical feedback. In mechanistic interpretability, for example, we can study models that exist today, try to understand something concrete, and discover where our intuitions were wrong. That seems valuable across a range of timelines, although you still have to ask whether your work will transfer to more capable systems.

And I’d distinguish the community’s allocation from an individual’s allocation. The community should be diversified; each person doesn’t need to split their week between five different agendas. You should consider your comparative advantage and where you can do unusually good work, alongside how important that work looks under different futures. Then revisit those judgements as we learn more.

r001.rationale: The response says empirical work can be valuable across timelines, but does not say that much safety work aimed at short timelines remains valuable under other assumptions.
